It is further contended that, there was a partition affected between four sons of Nanjundappa on 10.04.1972. In the said O.S. No.5782/2016 partition six items of agricultural property had fallen to the share of Muddappa, the father of the plaintiff and defendants, which are described in the plaint. It is averred that after the partition, mutation entries were made under MRNO. 14/1995-96 in respect of Sy. No. 47/1 measuring 14 guntas, MR No. 25/1995-96 in respect of Sy. The plaintiff and defendants are Hindus by religion and they are governed by Mithakashra law . It is averred that the plaintiff and defendants are in joint possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule property.

It is averred that the properties bearing Sy.No.100/1B measuring 4½ guntas of land O.S. No.5782/2016 has been acquired by BBMP for road widening purposes. The acquiring authority has awarded compensation to the extent of Rs.61,13,076/- and Rs.17,57,721/-. The defendants are trying to receive the entire award amount with out reference or obtaining consent from the plaintiff. It is further averred that the defendants are making hectic efforts to receive compensation from the acquiring body to defeat the rights of the plaintiff from receiving the award amount from the acquiring authority . It is averred that the the defendants have played fraud and misrepresentation on the plaintiff . Issue No.1 :- It is the case of the plaintiff that the suit schedule properties were acquired by their father Muddappa under the partition deed dated 10.04.1972, which was affected between four sons of Nanjundappa. A careful scrutiny of the materials on record reveal that the neither the claim of the plaintiff with the regard to the acquisition of the suit properties by Muddappa under the partition dated 10.4.1972 nor the O.S. No.5782/2016 claim of the plaintiff in the suit properties are disputed by the defendants. A conjoint reading of written statement averments at paragraph no. 4, 5 and 7 disclose that the defendants have categorically admitted the entitlement of the plaintiff to the extent of 1/3rd share in the suit properties but they have fundamentally defended the claim on the ground of non availability of the suit properties for partition. No doubt Section 53 of the Bharatiya Sakhsya Adhiniyam, 2023 ( herein after referred as BSA) the erstwhile Section 58 Indian Evidence Act, 1872, provides that no fact needs to be proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their agents agree to admit at the hearing, or which, before the hearing, they agree to admit by any writing under their hands, or which by any rule of pleading in force at the time they are deemed to have admitted by their pleadings but the proviso of Section 53 of the BSA provides that the Court may, in its discretion, require the facts admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admissions. In the above case the plaintiff has not pleaded the details of the O.S. No.5782/2016 acquisition of the suit properties from her great grand father in the plaint or produced any other documents evidencing the flow of title under Section 6 of the Amended Hindu Succession Act, 1956 . Meanwhile the issue no.1 framed by the court indicates that this court has not chosen to hold that the suit properties are the ancestral properties owing to the judicial admission of the defendants in the written statement but instead the court has directed the parties to lead evidence and consequentially the evidence led Sulochana M vs Mahesh M on 28 January, 2026 in this context has to be examined notwithstanding the defendants' admission in the written statement on the mode of acquisition of the suit properties by Mudappa.

In the instant case the plaintiff is claiming the right through her deceased father namely Mudappa without indicating that the suit properties were acquired through her paternal ancestors upto three degrees above her. The Hon'ble Apex Court of India between Arshnoor Singh V/s Harpal Kaur and Others, reported in (2020) 14 SCC 436 at para 7.3 held that under Mitakshara law, whenever a male ancestor inherits any O.S. No.5782/2016 property from any of his paternal ancestors upto three degrees above him, then his male legal heirs upto three degrees below him, would get an equal right as coparceners in that property. The Hon'ble Apex Court of India in Vineeta Sharma V/s Rakesh Sharma & Others (Supra) at Page 34 Para 24 has held that a coparcenary property is the one which is inherited by a Hindu from his father, grandfather, or great grandfather. Property inherited from others is held in his rights and cannot be treated as forming part of the coparcenary. The property in coparcenary is held as joint owners. The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in RFA NO. 1925/2006 in the case of Basavaraj Meti and another v. Prema bai Jamadar and others, while answering the point on whether the property inherited under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, acquires the characteristic of a co- paracenery property subsequent to the division of properties between two brothers vis-à-vis sons of the parties to the partition, has held that coparcenary is a creature of the statute and it cannot be created by way of an agreement. That being the O.S. No.5782/2016 position the conduct of the parties will not change the characteristics of the property. It is appropriate to extract para 18 of the above judgment : "18.

It is required to be noticed that the Act is watershed movement when it comes to succession among Hindus. The Act deals with both testamentary as well as non-testamentary succession both in respect of coparcenary properties as well as self acquired properties. In addition to that, Section 4 of the Act has a far reaching consequence as the said provision has an overriding effect in respect of all matters for which the provision is made in the Act. As far as succession is concerned,there is no dispute that Sections 6, 8, 15 and 1 9 of the Act are the provisions governing the succession to the properties of a Hindu. From reading of these provisions, it is abundantly clear that the parliament in its wisdom wanted to do away with the concept of the birth right in respect of properties governed under Section 8 of the Act. This being the position, this Court is of the view that merely because Kanaksingh and Raghunathsingh effected a partition between themselves in respect of the properties which they inherited under Section 8 of the Act, the character of the property will not change. The nature of the property has to be determined with reference to the nature of acquisition after the O.S. No.5782/2016 demise of the holder of the property. If the holder of the property dies leaving behind the self acquired property, then the property would devolve under Section 8 of the Act. If the holder dies leaving behind his share in the coparcenary property, then Section 6 of the Act would come into picture provided other circumstances enumerated in Section 6 of the Act are met with.". From the above judgments it is pellucid that in order to claim a share in the coparcenary property the plaintiff has to necessarily prove that the property sought to be partitioned is a Mitakshara coparcenary property inherited from his paternal ancestors upto three degrees above him. In the case on hand it is not the case of the plaintiff that suit properties were the coparcenary property of her great grandfather and the father of the plaintiff had acquired rights over the suit properties under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. There is nothing on record to prove that the great grand father of the plaintiff had acquired the suit properties from his paternal ancestors upto three degrees above him. .When the plaintiff is O.S. No.5782/2016 claiming coparcenary rights in the suit properties it is incumbent upon the plaintiff to plead and prove that her father leaving behind his share in the coparcenary property.

The plaint averments are bereft of the material particulars of the same. Mere plea of partition between the children of Nanjundappa on 10.4.1972 without providing any material particulars of the mode of acquisition of the properties is not sufficient to hold that the suit properties are the ancestral and coparcenary properties. The execution of the partition deed between the family members in respect of properties left behind by the holder of the properties would not change the character of the properties from self acquired properties to that of coparcenary properties. As held in the above judgments coparcenary is a creature of the statute and it cannot be created by way of an agreement and thus no presumption of coparcenary property can be drawn. It is not the case of the plaintiff that properties devolved upon the children of Nanjundappa were inherited from their paternal ancestors up O.S. No.5782/2016 to three degrees above them and they had affected partition in respect of such properties . Even the genealogical tree produced by the plaintiff at Ex.P1 does not go beyond Nanjundappa, who is the paternal grand father of the plaintiff. There are no particulars specifying the names of the paternal ancestors of the plaintiff in the family tree upto three degrees above the plaintiff in the plaint. Ex.P3 and P4 merely disclose that the properties allotted to Mudappa in respect of Sy. NO. 47/1 , Sy. NO. 256/3 and Sy. NO. 261/2 on the basis of the partition on 10.4.1972 were mutated in the revenue records. None of the documents produced by the plaintiff in the form of RTC extracts and encumbrance certificates would be of any assistance to prove the the suit properties are the ancestral properties .

A perusal of the RTC extracts produced at Ex.P5 to 17 , Ex.P23 to 26, Ex.P51, Ex.P52, Ex.P55 , Ex.P 57, Ex.P58, Ex.P61 standing in the name of Malleshaih with reference to Sy. NO. 167/3 , 167/2 , Sy. No. 256/3 & P56; the RTC extracts standing in the name of Nanjundappa at Ex.P19 & 21with reference to Sy. No. 47/1 ; the RTC extract at Ex.P53 & 59 in respect of Sy. No. 256/3 in the name of Puttamariayyappa , Mudappa and Gouramma , the RTC extract at Ex.P54, 60 in respect of Sy. No. 261/ 2 in the name of Puttaiah and Mudappa; Similarly the RTC extracts at Ex.P27 and 28 which disclose the name of Malleshaiah, Puttaiah, Puttamarriappa and Mudappa in respect of Sy. No. 256/3 or the RTC extracts at Ex.P29 and 30 standing in the name of Puttaiah and Mudappa in respect of Sy. No. 261/2, would not come to the aid and assistance of the plaintiff to substantiate that the suit properties are the ancestral and coparcenary properties. In State of Himachal Pradesh Vs. Keshar Ram and others, reported in 1996 (11) SCC 257 the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that "the entries in the revenue papers, by no stretch of imagination can from the basis for declaration of title in favour of the plaintiff". The Hon'ble O.S. No.5782/2016 Supreme Court further held that even if the entries in record of rights carry Sulochana M vs Mahesh M on 28 January, 2026 evidentiary value, that itself would not confer any title on the plaintiff on the suit land in question.

Thus even if some of the properties are found to be standing in the name of Mudappa in the RTC extracts the same would not confer any coparcenary right on the plaintiff. Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act 1872 merely proves that consideration or object of an agreement should be lawful. Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act provides when, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise. There fore in view of the above definition the consideration for any contract need not be monetary consideration. Section 25 of the Indian Contract Act further provides that agreement without consideration is void unless it is in writing and registered or is a promise to compensate for something done or is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation of law. Under this provision it is very much pellucid that when an agreement without consideration is registered under the law then inspite of the absence of consideration, the agreement is valid. Therefore the contention O.S. No.5782/2016 that the relinquishment deed is liable to be can celled for want of consideration is not sustainable.

On a plain reading of the above provision , it is evident that the proviso is not applicable to Wills and consequently the Will cannot be used as evidence until one of the attesting witness has been called for the purpose of proving its execution. It is material to note that the said proviso does not state of situation where a Will is not in dispute and consequentially the effect of Section 58 of the Indian Evidence Act or Section 53 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. is not taken away. In the absence of any exclusion in terms of O.S. No.5782/2016 applicability of Section 53 of the BSA under Section 67 of the BSA, the provisions of Section 67 of the BSA have to be given effect to by considering its true spirit and intent. Section 67 relates to those documents which require to be proved at the trial of a suit. If by any rule of law or of pleadings, such proof is not required, Section 67 cannot operate to insist on formal proof by calling an attesting witness. Section 53 has to be read as overriding Section 67 and as obviating the necessity for calling an attesting witness, unless the execution of the Will or the attestation is in dispute. O.S. No.5782/2016

The limitation period under Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is three years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument or decree canceled or set aside or the contract rescinded first become known to him. But the explanation - 3 of T.P.Act provides that a registration of a document is deemed knowledge of the factum of registration. In Janardhanam Prasad v. Ramdas (2007) 15 SCC 174, the Supreme Court relying on Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 has held that a person is said to have notice' of a fact when he actually knows that fact, or when but for wilful absentation from an enquiry or search which he ought to have made , or gross negligence, he would have known it.The explanation of Section 3 further provides that, any person acquiring any immovable property or any part of, or share or interest in, such property shall be deemed to have notice of the title if any person who is for time being in actual possession thereof. It is held that the principle of constructive notice is applicable in respect of registered instrument. The plaintiff has O.S.
